extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning introductory set theory, quantificational logic, and proof-writing
extracted.subtask_description: Instructional guidance for translating set-theoretic notation into formal logical formulas and for constructing elementary mathematical proofs. Covers set-builder and indexed-family notation, power sets, unions/intersections of families, strategies for choosing definitions, and basic proof techniques (e.g., assume-to-prove conditionals, tracking givens/goals, avoiding unjustified assertions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-builder notation equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: The notation {n^2 | n ∈ N} can be rewritten using an elementhood test as {x | ∃n ∈ N(x = n^2)}, so x ∈ {n^2 | n ∈ N} means the same thing as ∃n ∈ N(x = n^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a set is described by an expression in the left of the vertical bar, you may replace it by a variable and add an existential quantifier equating the variable to that expression. Examples show converting {n^2 | n ∈ N} to {x | ∃n ∈ N(x = n^2)}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexed families and index sets
rubrics_metrics.description: A set written as {x_i | i ∈ I} (an indexed family) can be defined equivalently as {x | ∃i ∈ I (x = x_i)}. The index set I identifies each element x_i; indices need not be numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may often simplify subset or membership statements by either expanding x ∈ {x_i | i∈I} to ∃i(x = x_i) or by quantifying over indices (e.g., ∀i∈I (x_i ∈ A)). Examples include numbered primes p1,...,p100 and mothers ms for students s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Families of sets (sets whose elements are sets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anything at all can be an element of a set, including sets; e.g., F = {A, B, C} where A, B, C are themselves sets. Membership (∈) and subset relations must be kept distinct: 1 ∈ A and A ∈ F but 1 ∉ F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working with families of sets remember the elements of the family are sets themselves (e.g., Cs = set of courses student s has taken) and avoid confusing elementhood with subsethood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power set definition and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: P(A) is the set whose elements are all subsets of A: P(A) = {x | x ⊆ A}. For example P({7,12}) = {∅, {7}, {12}, {7,12}} and P(∅) = {∅}. Note {∅} ≠ ∅.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To say x ∈ P(A) translate to x ⊆ A, i.e., ∀y(y ∈ x → y ∈ A). Keep in mind that subsets of X are elements of P(X), so families of subsets are subsets of P(X) (e.g., F ⊆ P(C)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Union and intersection of a family of sets
rubrics_metrics.description: For a family F of sets define ∩F = {x | ∀A ∈ F(x ∈ A)} and ∪F = {x | ∃A ∈ F(x ∈ A)}. These generalize binary ∩ and ∪; when F = {A,B} these reduce to A ∩ B and A ∪ B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate membership in ∩F as a universal quantifier over the family and membership in ∪F as an existential quantifier. Note some mathematicians consider ∩F undefined when F = ∅; the text uses ∩F only when F ≠ ∅.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outermost-symbol translation rule
rubrics_metrics.description: When unpacking a complex set-theoretic expression into logic, a good rule of thumb is to start with the 'outermost' symbol and expand its definition first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose which definition to think about first based on the nesting of symbols: e.g., if intersection occurs inside a power set, expand power set first (Example 2.3.3 vs 2.3.3(5)). Doing this judiciously simplifies translations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translating membership statements into logical formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Many set-theoretic membership statements can be translated into quantified logical formulas (e.g., x ∈ P(A) → ∀y(y ∈ x → y ∈ A); x ∈ P(A ∩ B) → ∀y(y ∈ x → (y ∈ A ∧ y ∈ B)); x ∈ ∪F → ∃A ∈ F(x ∈ A)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow definitions step-by-step: write the meaning of the set notation (power set, union, intersection, subset) in terms of ∀ and ∃ and basic predicates. Use these translations to test truth or falsehood efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative equivalent formulations for subsets
rubrics_metrics.description: To show {x_i | i ∈ I} ⊆ A you may either write ∀x(∃i ∈ I(x = x_i) → x ∈ A) or equivalently ∀i ∈ I (x_i ∈ A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both forms are equivalent; choose the one that makes the argument simpler. Demonstrating equivalence may require later techniques (Chapter 3 references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional proof strategy (prove P → Q by assuming P)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a conclusion of the form P → Q: assume P is true and then prove Q. Treat the assumption P as an additional hypothesis (a given) for the remainder of that part of the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This transformation changes the goal from P → Q to Q while adding P to the givens; after deriving Q under that assumption you have shown P → Q. Use this as a step in composing larger proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Givens and goal bookkeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: During proof construction, call the currently known or assumed statements 'givens' and the statement still to be proved the 'goal'. Both givens and goal may change as you apply proof strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track transformations by updating givens and the goal. Many proof strategies operate by changing the goal or adding givens (assumptions) to make the problem easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never assert without justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Never assert anything until you can justify it completely using the hypotheses or earlier conclusions. Motto: 'I shall make no assertion before its time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents circular reasoning and unjustified leaps. Be skeptical about every inference; if it doesn't convince you, it won't convince others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish assumptions from assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming a statement P for the sake of argument is not the same as asserting P is true. Conclusions derived from an assumption only show 'if P then ...' unless P is independently justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you assume P to derive Q you have proved P → Q, not Q outright. Only assert conclusions when adequately justified by givens or proven lemmas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use counterexamples to disprove incorrect theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: A single instance (assignment of values) where the hypotheses are true but the conclusion is false constitutes a counterexample and shows the theorem is incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a purported theorem fails, provide a concrete counterexample (e.g., for 'Suppose x > 3. Then x^2 − 2y > 5' take x=4, y=6 to get counterexample). Finding counterexamples is definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof is deductive argument from hypotheses to conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof of a theorem is a deductive argument whose premises are the hypotheses of the theorem and whose conclusion is the theorem's conclusion; the argument must be valid so the conclusion follows whenever hypotheses hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing a proof requires justifying each step from givens or previously established results; the goal is to guarantee the conclusion whenever the hypotheses are true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic/operational manipulations must respect conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: When manipulating inequalities or other relations be mindful of conditions (e.g., multiplying both sides of an inequality by a positive number preserves the direction; by a negative reverses it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose operations that are valid under given assumptions. Example: to prove 0 < a < b implies a^2 < b^2 multiply by positive numbers a and b to get a^2 < ab < b^2 and conclude a^2 < b^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexed notation alternatives and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: For an indexed family F = {A_i | i ∈ I}, alternative notation ∩_{i∈I} A_i and ∪_{i∈I} A_i denotes ∩F and ∪F respectively, with ∩_{i∈I} A_i = {x | ∀i∈I(x∈A_i)} and ∪_{i∈I} A_i = {x | ∃i∈I(x∈A_i)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use indexed notation for compactness (e.g., ∩_{s∈S} C_s). When translating or proving identities, expand these into quantifiers over indices as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care with empty-indexed intersections and unions
rubrics_metrics.description: If F = ∅ then ∪F = ∅ (x ∈ ∪F is always false) and x ∈ ∩F is true for every x (leading some to treat ∩∅ as the universe U); to avoid ambiguity the book uses ∩F only when F ≠ ∅.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about universes of discourse if you wish to define ∩∅; otherwise avoid using ∩∅ to prevent context-dependent meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational caution: universe of all sets and Russell's paradox
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming a 'set of all sets' U leads to contradiction: define R = {A ∈ U | A ∉ A} and apply self-reference to derive Russell's Paradox, showing naive 'universe of all sets' assumptions are problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of foundational subtleties when sets have sets as elements; do not casually assume the existence of a set-of-all-sets. Reflect on the implications for set theory foundations.
